entry.title: Brian Schottenheimer is keeping poor company right now
entry.summary: It has only been 22 games, to be clear. But right now Brian Schottenheimer is in some poor company. The company in question is as things relate to Dallas Cowboys franchise history. Schottenheimer has led the team through a full season and five games of another, and in both instances he failed to win a […]
entry.content:
It has only been 22 games, to be clear. But right now Brian Schottenheimer is in some poor company. The company in question is as things relate to Dallas Cowboys franchise history.

Schottenheimer has led the team through a full season and five games of another, and in both instances he failed to win a majority of his first five games.

This isn’t an arbitrary mark chosen, to be clear. Stathead and Pro Football Reference only allow searching spans to begin a season that are at least five games in length, and now that the Cowboys are through that point we can really measure Schottenheimer against those who came before him.

Here is every team in Dallas Cowboys franchise history to hold two or fewer wins through their first five games. This specific wording allows us to capture the tie from Week 5 last year.

The Cowboys have held two or fewer wins through five games a total of 24 times now. They made the playoffs only twice in the previous 23 instances. Not great.

What is interesting is if we consider the head coaches who, like Brian Schottenheimer, did this in consecutive seasons. It is quite (not really) the list.

Dallas Cowboys head coaches to lead the team to two or fewer wins through the first five games in consecutive seasons:

  • Brian Schottenheimer
  • Jason Garrett
  • Dave Campo
  • Jimmy Johnson
  • Tom Landry

Again, apologies for the specific wording. 2-2-1 is not the same thing as 2-3, but I think we all agree that in an effective sense it is. Moving on.

Brian Schottenheimer is either going to be Jason Garrett or Dave Campo… or Jimmy Johnson or Tom Landry. Based on this at least.

Many will likely say that the reason the latter pair dealt with starts of this variety is because of the day and age they played in as well as the fact that when they each took over they did so when the franchise was at very low points. That is more than fair. Briain Schottenheimer hardly inherited an expansion team or one with the number one overall pick.

Things are taking on water in a very serious sense for the Cowboys right now and if Schottenheimer doesn’t sort them out then he really is going to be associated with names that people do not regard all too fondly.

Time is running out.

entry.title: Cowboys news: Team adds defensive help to coaching staff
entry.summary: The Dallas Cowboys losing on Thursday night at home to the previously winless Buccaneers was somehow not the most embarrassing thing to happen throughout the NFC East in week five. The Philadelphia Eagles had their own international meltdown involving a late field goal to lose, in London to the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Commanders ran the […]
entry.content:
The Dallas Cowboys losing on Thursday night at home to the previously winless Buccaneers was somehow not the most embarrassing thing to happen throughout the NFC East in week five. The Philadelphia Eagles had their own international meltdown involving a late field goal to lose, in London to the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Commanders ran the clock out on themselves with a chance to beat the first place New York Giants in overtime.

The 2-3 Cowboys are still in the playoff race as a result, but they need to avoid further coaching mistakes like the rest of their rivals. The organization hired Mike Pettine to help first year defensive coordinator Christian Parker on Monday to help with this.

Cowboys add Mike Pettine to defensive coaching staff – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com

The Cowboys had visions of Christian Parker working with veteran coach Mike Pettine for some time, and hired the former Packers coach ahead of a primetime game in Green Bay.

Mike Pettine has been added as senior defensive assistant — a former defensive coordinator of the New York Jets, Buffalo Bills and the Green Bay Packers, and he most recently worked with the Minnesota Vikings to help Brian Flores form one of the more formidable defenses in the league.

“Had a chance to work with Pettine for a number of years, along with the Jets, and he’s gonna be here in a role to support everything that [Christian Parker] is leading and guiding, and we are really, really excited,” Schottenheimer said on Monday. “They worked together in Green Bay, and this is actually something the C.P. and I talked about when we first hired him.”

What a horrific NFL week 5 for the NFC East – Shane Tayl0r, Inside The Star

Kickoff strategy in late-game situations will be a real discussion point between the Cowboys and Eagles, who play each other in Week 7.

A 48-yard field goal for Philly gave them a 19-17 lead with eight seconds remaining.

However, Jags returner Ameer Abdullah returned the ensuing kickoff 53 yards to set up Cam Little with a 57-yard field goal. So, instead of kicking the ball into the end zone, forcing the Jags to have to run a play on offense with no timeouts, head coach of the Eagles, Nick Sirianni, kept it in play and allowed legit the only thing that could have beat you happen.

NFL Week 5 Sunday aftermath: Commanders melt down in tie; Eagles rue costly last-second gaffe – Kevin Patra, NFL.com

Nick Sirianni took the blame for the Eagles late loss the same way Brian Schottenheimer did after Thursday night.

Sirianni likely had the Week 3 Ravens-Cowboys ending in his brain at the time, wherein Dallas kicked to the end zone, which allowed Baltimore to run a play and get into field goal range in six seconds for a stunning game-winner. The difference here was that Jacksonville didn’t have a timeout. That detail is massive.

Without a timeout, even starting at the 35-yard line, Jacksonville would have had to throw at a presumably well-guarded boundary to stop the clock. Not impossible, but harder than the helter-skelter kick returns can create. That Philly allowed a big return that was called back to start the game — and was missing a key special teams player in Jeremiah Trotter Jr., who earlier was ejected for fighting — should also have played a role in Sirianni’s thinking.

After slow growth, Cowboys defense struggles vs lowly Bucs – Dyllan Rivers, Blogging The Boys

The way the Cowboys allowed explosive plays against the Bucs in the second half was highly concerning.

On the first play of the second half, Bucky Irving broke free on a run that seemed to take an eternity to cross the line of scrimmage, finally taken down by Caleb Downs after a 72-yard scamper. The very next play resulted in a Tampa Bay touchdown. Two plays, 86 yards, seven points.

The next drive, coming after a Ryan Flournoy tipped ball interception, blew open on a Tez Johnson 64-yard catch and run. DaRon Bland tripped over his own feet, allowing Johnson to run free deep into Cowboys territory. After three back-to-back run plays, the Buccaneers would go on to score another touchdown.

Enough time has passed for us to point out the 3 silver linings from the Dallas Cowboys’ loss to the Bucs in Week 5 – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports

CeeDee Lamb was quiet in the Thursday night home game, but it meant George Pickens finally got going. Is Dallas closer to having both receivers go off in the same game?

No one should have been overly concerned. This is the way the Cowboys offense will operate as long as it has two elite wide receivers. Still, a strong performance from Pickens is good for everyone in Dallas, and mostly for his confidence.

He finished with nine catches for 130 yards and a touchdown on 13 targets. The Cowboys went to him on the slant a lot once again. He probably wants a few of those targets back, but beyond the numbers, Pickens kept showing up when the Cowboys needed him the most.

entry.title: History says this Cowboys team is doomed
entry.summary: The Dallas Cowboys have played five games so far this season and unfortunately won only a pair of them. 40% success is hardly worth bragging about. In more specific terms, a 2-3 record is a tough scene. To be clear, the first five weeks of the season were arguably the most difficult in terms of […]
entry.content:
The Dallas Cowboys have played five games so far this season and unfortunately won only a pair of them. 40% success is hardly worth bragging about.

In more specific terms, a 2-3 record is a tough scene. To be clear, the first five weeks of the season were arguably the most difficult in terms of any five-week stretch. This was the case because of the travel to Brazil, the road game after, and the short week that followed that. This is for context only and in no way to excuse what the Cowboys have done during the span in question.

If the Cowboys held four wins through this stretch, they would likely be a playoff team this season. Obviously they came nowhere close to that. More practically speaking, emerging from this stretch 3-2 would be a huge win, again relative to the unique quirks of the schedule. They didn’t even get there.

Unfortunately with a 2-3 record at their backs, they are also now facing an uphill battle from a historical perspective.

History says this team won’t make the playoffs

With five weeks now in the books we can search certain things at Stathead and Pro Football Reference that weren’t as easily accessible before. Their system doesn’t allow for searches that include spans to start a season short of five games.

Here is a list of every team in franchise history that has started their season with a 2-3 (or worse) record. This year’s team is number 24 in that capacity.

Of the previous 2-3 instances where a Cowboys team was 2-3 or worse through the first five games, they have only made the playoffs twice. If we round up that is 9%.

You’ll note that each of those two teams (1996 and 2018) saw the Cowboys reach the postseason as the NFC East winner. Some years it pays to be in a crummy division, and that certainly seems to be the case this year for Dallas. On the heels of what we saw in Week 5, 10 wins probably earns some hats and t-shirts for whoever gets there. Maybe it will be the Cowboys.

But this does not bode well! If you look at the list of teams on this list and reference them against what you remember about each of them, you will realize that we are talking about some Cowboys teams that were not very good and who were actually particularly maddening.

On the latter note, part of what is frustrating about this is that the Cowboys are here in consecutive seasons (they were actually 2-2-1 last year to be clear) despite an offense that, on paper, is one of the best in franchise history. That they are not able to capitalize on that through over a full season now is an endless mystery.

Do you think the Cowboys will be part of the 9% when this season is over? Or will they fall among the rest? Let us know in the comments below.

entry.title: Cowboys hiring NFL veteran with Christian Parker background to defensive staff
entry.summary: The scramble is on for the Dallas Cowboys Five games into the season, it has become obvious that something has to change. You can make this declaration about any part of the team to be honest, but defense is sort of the spot of major concern. It was reported on Monday that the Cowboys have […]
entry.content:
The scramble is on for the Dallas Cowboys

Five games into the season, it has become obvious that something has to change. You can make this declaration about any part of the team to be honest, but defense is sort of the spot of major concern.

It was reported on Monday that the Cowboys have made a move there, so to speak. Mike Pettine is joining the Cowboys defensive staff, according to multiple reports.

It should be noted that Pettine, and Parker for that matter, was on the Packers staff in 2018 under Mike McCarthy. We all know that McCarthy was dismissed before that season ended and that in 2020 he joined the Cowboys.

Including that Parker tried to originally hire Pettine when joining the Cowboys himself sounds like some positive spin, but we obviously don’t know anything beyond this report. Whatever the case, Pettine is on board.

Can he singlehandedly fix or at least help fix what is going on? That remains to be seen. At the very least he has experience that Christian Parker doesn’t in terms of running an NFL defense.

The Cowboys can clearly use all of the help that they can get.

entry.title: After slow growth, Cowboys defense struggles vs lowly Bucs
entry.summary: The Dallas Cowboys defense let up their second lowest point total of the season while simultaneously having one of their worst games. Let’s take a look at how they performed this week. Team stats allowed Against the Buccaneers, the Cowboys defense allowed three touchdowns and one field goal. 17 of the 24 points allowed came […]
entry.content:
The Dallas Cowboys defense let up their second lowest point total of the season while simultaneously having one of their worst games. Let’s take a look at how they performed this week.

Team stats allowed

Against the Buccaneers, the Cowboys defense allowed three touchdowns and one field goal. 17 of the 24 points allowed came in the third quarter.

Tampa Bay ran for 241 yards on 39 attempts, good for an average of 6.2 yards on the day. Two of the three touchdowns scored would come from the rushing attack.

The Buccaneers would end the day with 24 first downs, a 53.8% conversion rate on third down, and a 60% touchdown rate in the redzone.

The Cowboys defense struggled getting off the field, allowing Tampa Bay to hold the ball for nearly 40 minutes.

Individual stat leaders on defense

Dee Winters finished with a team high ten tackles, six of which were solo.

Otito Ogbonnia led the team in tackles for loss with two.

Rookie Malachi Lawrence found his first NFL sack on the day.

Advanced analytics

The highest graded players on the day per Pro Football Focus were Markquese Bell (81.2), Malik Hooker (75.9), and Malachi Lawrence (74.4).

The lowest graded players were DaRon Bland (29.6), Shavon Revel (36.9), and Kenny Clark (41.7).

The Buccaneers cashed in on explosive plays, generating seven on Thursday night. Two of the biggest explosives on the day, Bucky Irving’s 72-yard run and Tez Johnson’s 64-yard reception, led to touchdowns in the third quarter.

How’d the rookies look?

Caleb Downs finished the game with four tackles, but also missed two on the night. Injuries are forcing him to sit back and play deep safety, which is an unfortunate waste of his talent. Once the Cowboys’ secondary begins to get healthy, expect to see Downs back to his normal role at nickel. His impact in run support around the line of scrimmage has been missed.

Jaishawn Barham recorded seven tackles and one miss. He also had another goal line stand this week, sparking life into a team hanging on by a thread. The rookie linebacker continues to be an important piece in the middle of the defense.

Malachi Lawrence was the best of the Cowboys rookie class on Thursday. He recorded his first sack of the season, while also adding three pressures and a pass defended on the night. As Dallas’ most productive pass rusher, Lawrence should continue to see his role increase as the season continues.

LT Overton had 23 snaps this week, generating one pressure and recording one tackle. He flashes on tape, but hasn’t had a huge impact on the box score. He’s a potential bright spot down the road when he sees an increase in snaps.

Final grade: F

Christian Parker and his defense entered Thursday Night Football with a massive opportunity for a get right game. They started their night on defense by allowing a seven point Tampa Bay drive that consumed nearly an entire quarter. After that they buckled down they forced three punts before the half was over. Things were looking up on defense.

But then the third quarter began.

On the first play of the second half, Bucky Irving broke free on a run that seemed to take an eternity to cross the line of scrimmage, finally taken down by Caleb Downs after a 72-yard scamper. The very next play resulted in a Tampa Bay touchdown. Two plays, 86 yards, seven points.

The next drive, coming after a Ryan Flournoy tipped ball interception, blew open on a Tez Johnson 64-yard catch and run. DaRon Bland tripped over his own feet, allowing Johnson to run free deep into Cowboys territory. After three back-to-back run plays, the Buccaneers would go on to score another touchdown.

The final points in the third quarter would come from a field goal after a KaVontae Turpin special teams fumble. A commendable effort by the defense on a drive that started at the Dallas 37.

Those two explosive plays by Irving and Johnson, however, changed everything.

In addition to the explosives, Dallas finished the game with 12 missed tackles. Could this be a result of schedule exhaustion? Traveling to Rio to get beat up by a physical Ravens offense, returning to face off against a winless-but-tough Texans team, and then playing again just four days later surely played a role.

But the Cowboys were still a clear favorite for a reason. And to allow an undrafted rookie free agent quarterback to not only survive, but to thrive, is a travesty. In no world should Jalon Daniels finish with a 76% completion rating and a 40 point higher quarterback rating than Dak Prescott. And that’s no insult to the Buccaneers quarterback – this just isn’t a league that normally allows players in his position to play as well as he played.

Daniels even attempted to give the game away late, throwing a short pass into the arms of DaRon Bland. But the veteran corner rejected the potential game-tying gift, dropping the interception and leaving Cowboys fans across the globe screaming in agony.

The Cowboys didn’t pressure the quarterback enough. The secondary constantly made mistakes, including a 22-yard gain on 3rd-and-21. And the 12 missed tackles contributed to the massive Buccaneers day on the ground.

Allowing 24 points is one of the few positives on the day. With an offense as good as Dallas has, there won’t be many games this team loses when holding opponents to that total or less. It should have been enough to win this game (my score prediction was 34-24), but the offense had a surprisingly tough night as well.

When considering the winless opponent, their undrafted rookie quarterback starting just his second game, and the struggles Tampa Bay has had in pass protection, this should have been a game the Cowboys defense would use to right the ship. Instead they surrendered an unconscionable amount of yards on the ground and allowed the rookie quarterback to live free of pressure for most of the night.

For these reasons, this defense gets their first F of the season. There is hope for better days brought by the return of injured players on defense and the insertion of Joey Porter Jr. into the lineup. We may also see some changes, with Brian Schottenheimer vowing to shake things up.

Next week, Dallas travels to Lambeau Field to take on Jordan Love and the Packers on Sunday Night Football. We’ll see if the Christian Parker’s defense can begin to right the ship against Green Bay’s 28th ranked scoring offense.

entry.title: Struggling Jake Ferguson keeps dropping the ball for the Cowboys
entry.summary: Since stepping into the starting role in 2023, tight end Jake Ferguson has cemented himself as a key component of the Dallas Cowboys’ offense. His quick emergence allowed the team to transition away from Dalton Schultz to Ferguson at a much lower price. The young tight end quickly earned the trust of Dak Prescott, establishing […]
entry.content:
Since stepping into the starting role in 2023, tight end Jake Ferguson has cemented himself as a key component of the Dallas Cowboys’ offense. His quick emergence allowed the team to transition away from Dalton Schultz to Ferguson at a much lower price. The young tight end quickly earned the trust of Dak Prescott, establishing himself as a reliable safety valve and a vibrant source of energy for the offense.

Through his first four years in the league, he put together two Pro Bowl seasons as he found ways to find soft spots in coverage and make the most of every reception with impressive toughness and the occasional hurdle of defenders. Having a seam-stretching tight end who commanded attention helped make a dynamic Cowboys offense even more dynamic. Fans loved him.

Last July, Ferguson signed a four-year, $52 million extension with the team, putting him under team control through the 2029 season. While his athleticism and locker room energy made him a guy the team wanted to hold on to, a pattern of costly mistakes is starting to raise questions about his overall consistency and long-term effectiveness.

In past seasons, the veteran tight end has shown good hands, making contested catches look effortless, but recently his focus has wavered at critical moments. Through five games this year, he has a drop rate of 9.5%, which is a high percentage for a player targeted on short-to-intermediate routes. Obviously, the most devastating example came on Thursday night when the ball was thrown right at his grill. Not only did he not secure the catch, but the ball deflected off his face and stayed in the air forever until a Buccaneers defender could safely get under it. A potential comeback drive turned into a costly game-ending mistake.

Even more alarming than the periodic drop is Ferguson’s ongoing battle with ball security after the catch. Over the last three years, he’s put the ball on the turf a staggering eight times, leading all tight ends in that span. That’s a rate of once every 19.6 times he touches the ball. For perspective, that is like a running back who touches the ball 20 times a game who fumbles once every game. That’s atrocious.

His fumbling woes have caused opposing defensive coordinators to openly admit to going after him. Ferguson has a bad habit of carrying the ball away from his frame, making him vulnerable to aggressive defenders who deliberately swipe at the ball. And it’s worked. He had a costly fumble on a shovel pass against the Baltimore Ravens a couple of weeks ago that erased a promising scoring drive. We can argue until we are blue in the face about whether that should’ve been ruled incomplete, but either way, Ferguson isn’t doing a good job securing the ball.

These things are harmful to the team, but some might be willing to give him a little leniency if he were a strong blocker. He’s not. His chip blocks are ineffective, and he routinely misses his blocking assignments in the running game. There are more and more instances of Ferguson being tossed aside as a blocker. It’s not good.

The Cowboys invested a second-round pick in Luke Schoonmaker in 2023, but he has not worked out as planned. The team reupped on Ferguson, but now, suddenly, he has created a bit of concern as well. The front office also wisely extended Brevyn Spann-Ford, who is the team’s gritty blocker and special teams contributor, but one can’t help wondering if we could see a change in responsibilities as the season moves forward. If Ferguson can’t clean up some of his problems and start being more of a net positive than a liability, the Cowboys might have some tough decisions ahead.

entry.title: Cowboys’ coaching staff isn’t providing answers to team’s problems
entry.summary: At some point, a bad loss stops being an isolated incident and starts becoming a reflection of the people responsible for preventing it, going all the way up to the front office. Yet, since the Cowboys are structured and operated the way they are that’s a story for another day. For now, the focus should […]
entry.content:
At some point, a bad loss stops being an isolated incident and starts becoming a reflection of the people responsible for preventing it, going all the way up to the front office. Yet, since the Cowboys are structured and operated the way they are that’s a story for another day. For now, the focus should be on the field with the people who are making decisions in real-time.

Thursday night’s 24-16 defeat to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was another reminder that the problems plaguing this team extend far beyond one player, one position group or one unfortunate bounce of the football. Dallas lost at home to an 0-4 team starting an undrafted rookie quarterback in his second NFL start. Tampa Bay left AT&T Stadium with its first win of the season after outgaining Dallas in yardage, controlling possession for more than 39 minutes and winning the turnover battle 3-0.

The Cowboys once again struggled to stop the run, failed to sustain their offense, surrendered a costly special-teams turnover and watched their final realistic opportunity disappear when Jake Ferguson couldn’t secure a pass that became the game-sealing interception.

Individual mistakes played a role, but they cannot explain away the broader failure. Dallas looked unprepared to handle Tampa’s pressure, unable to stop its rushing attack and incapable of consistently executing in any phase of the game. When those problems appear simultaneously, the scrutiny has to extend beyond the players making mistakes and toward the coaches responsible for preparing them.

Brian Schottenheimer, Christian Parker, Klayton Adams and Nick Sorensen all have different responsibilities, but Thursday exposed shortcomings across their respective units. Five games into the season, the Cowboys have given fans little reason to believe this staff can turn a talented roster into a consistently competitive team.

Brian Schottenheimer keeps coming up short

Schottenheimer’s responsibility extends beyond calling plays. As head coach, he sets the team’s standards, oversees its preparation and ultimately answers for the product Dallas puts on the field. As offensive play-caller, he also has a direct hand in an offense that struggles at inopportune times.

Dallas opened Thursday’s game with a promising touchdown drive, but managed only three additional points before its final touchdown with 5:26 remaining in the fourth quarter. Tampa’s pressure disrupted Dak Prescott, and the Cowboys never found a consistent counter until the game was nearly out of reach.

When Dallas can establish its preferred rhythm, the offense has enough talent to score against anyone. When an opponent disrupts that rhythm, however, the Cowboys too often look as though they are waiting for the original plan to start working again rather than finding a different way to attack.

Every play-caller has bad games, but the better ones recognize when an opponent has taken away the first option and respond before an entire half slips away. Schottenheimer’s offense failed to do that against Tampa, and Dallas finished with three turnovers while leaving too much of the burden on Prescott to manufacture a comeback.

The struggles were not limited to the play calls themselves. TE Jake Ferguson’s blocking has been inconsistent, and his three-catch, 19-yard performance against Tampa ended with a drop that became an interception when Dallas was trying to mount a late comeback.

Not every tipped interception is the receiver’s fault, but Ferguson needed to secure a catchable pass in that situation. Combined with his ongoing difficulties as a blocker, the play highlighted another weakness the offense has not adequately addressed.

Ferguson has shown he can contribute as a receiver, but a tight end who struggles to finish blocks and cannot consistently deliver in critical moments puts his offense in difficult situations. The coaching staff must find a way to improve his execution or reconsider how heavily it relies on him. Continuing to use the same personnel in the same ways without addressing the results is not a meaningful adjustment.

Schottenheimer cannot catch passes or prevent every turnover, but he can put his players in better positions to succeed. His offense needs a more adaptable approach, and his team needs greater discipline in the situations that decide close games. Until those improvements become visible, it is fair to question whether he is the right person to lead this operation.

Christian Parker’s defense has no identity

If Schottenheimer’s offense failed to adjust, Christian Parker’s defense failed to stop the most obvious threat in front of it. Tampa Bay ran for 241 yards, with Bucky Irving accounting for 165 on 21 carries. Irving broke off a 72-yard run to open the second half, setting up a touchdown on the next play, and later added a one-yard scoring run. The Buccaneers finished with 419 total yards while controlling the game through their ground attack.

Meanwhile, quarterback Jalon Daniels completed 19 of 25 passes for 189 yards and a touchdown. He played efficiently without needing to take over the game, largely because Tampa could rely on its running game to move the chains and keep Dallas’ offense on the sideline.

That is an increasingly troubling reflection on Parker’s defense. Dallas entered the season expecting a new identity under a new coordinator, but the unit has struggled to stop the run, generate consistent pressure and create turnovers. Through five games, the Cowboys have yet to record an interception, although Daron Bland just tried his best to secure one.

In fairness, maybe Parker deserves some time to establish his system, and injuries have complicated his personnel decisions. Joey Porter Jr., acquired to strengthen the secondary, was unavailable Thursday because of an illness. Those circumstances deserve consideration, but they do not explain away the fundamental breakdowns against Tampa.

A defense should still be able to maintain gap discipline, tackle effectively and prevent an opponent from repeatedly exploiting the same weakness. The Buccaneers did all the things Dallas needed to prevent, and the Cowboys had no effective answer.

The performance also raised legitimate questions about the team’s preparation and effort, particularly on defense. Effort cannot be measured simply by looking at the final score, and a poor performance does not automatically mean players were unmotivated. But repeated failures to finish tackles, control the line of scrimmage and respond when Tampa seized momentum are difficult to overlook. These are fundamental responsibilities that should not disappear because an opponent has a favorable matchup or the game is being played on a short week.

Parker’s challenge is not simply to install a scheme; it is to establish a dependable standard of execution. The issue is not that he has failed to rebuild the defense in five games, but that his unit has yet to demonstrate a reliable foundation on which that rebuild can succeed.

Nick Sorensen’s special teams are another problem

Special teams should provide a hidden advantage when the offense and defense are struggling. Instead, Sorensen’s unit contributed another costly mistake to a night when Dallas could not afford to give away possessions.

After Tampa scored to take a 21-10 lead early in the third quarter, KaVontae Turpin fumbled the ensuing kickoff return. Tampa recovered at the Dallas 37-yard line and converted the short field into a 41-yard field goal, extending its lead to 24-10.

Turpin is responsible for securing the football, but the coaching staff also has to answer for a unit that failed to execute in a critical situation, again. Remember those blocked field goals in weeks 3 and 4? Sorensen’s job is to prepare the coverage and return units, reinforce fundamentals and limit precisely these kinds of mistakes.

The turnover was particularly damaging because Dallas needed an opportunity to respond after surrendering a quick touchdown. Instead, Tampa received another scoring chance without having to drive the length of the field. That is how a single special-teams error compounds the problems created by the other two phases.

Dallas cannot afford to keep surrendering possessions and field position while asking its offense to overcome defensive breakdowns. Sorensen’s unit has to become more dependable, because the Cowboys have little margin for mistakes when the rest of the team is struggling.

The Cowboys need answers, not more explanations

Five games are not enough to declare an entire season lost, and Dallas still has talent capable of producing better results. Prescott can move the football, the receiving corps has shown it can generate explosive plays, and the comeback against Houston demonstrated what the offense can accomplish when it finds its rhythm.

But the Tampa loss exposed how dependent Dallas is on individual talent to overcome its other weaknesses. When the offense struggled, the defense could not stop the run, and special teams handed away a possession. Ferguson’s late drop compounded the offensive problems, while the defense’s inability to get off the field left Dallas fighting an uphill battle for much of the night. There was no reliable phase of the team capable of compensating for the others.

That is the main problem with this coaching staff. Schottenheimer has not consistently demonstrated that he can adapt the offense or get the entire team to execute, or as he would say “play complementary football.”

Parker’s defense lacks a dependable identity, Adams’ offense needs better answers against pressure, and Sorensen’s unit cannot afford costly mistakes. Each coordinator has a different problem to solve, but the head coach is responsible for making sure those problems do not define the team as a whole.

The short week deserves some consideration, but it cannot serve as a blanket excuse for missed tackles, poor ball security, ineffective blocking and an inability to adjust, and simply put, beat a bad team at home. Dallas’ FO can continue, and will, to insist that it has the talent to compete, and there is evidence to support that claim.

What the Cowboys cannot keep doing is treating each disappointing performance as an isolated setback while the same fundamental issues resurface every week.

At some point, the staff has to demonstrate that it can turn those problems into progress. After Thursday night, Brian Schottenheimer and his coordinators have given Dallas very little reason to believe they are the answer.

entry.title: Empty promises and defensive meltdowns plague Cowboys
entry.summary: The Dallas Cowboys have descended into a deeply unsettling territory where their ongoing performances have become a recurring nightmare. For three straight weeks, we have gone into a game with this level of excitement only to realize that this team isn’t very good. They get us every time. How can we be such suckers! The […]
entry.content:
The Dallas Cowboys have descended into a deeply unsettling territory where their ongoing performances have become a recurring nightmare. For three straight weeks, we have gone into a game with this level of excitement only to realize that this team isn’t very good. They get us every time. How can we be such suckers!

The reason we fall for it is because they do have talent. Yes, more of that talent is on the offensive side of the ball, but there is no excuse for this team to be playing as poorly as they are. No excuse.

The loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was especially frustrating because the offense, supposedly the dependable side of this team, never found a comfortable rhythm. To be fair, the Bucs have a good defense, but there was still an expectation that Dallas would move the ball and create enough offense to control the game.

Instead, the Tampa defense brought pressure, put Dak Prescott in tough spots, and forced the Cowboys into uncomfortable situations. Prescott had escaped a few dangerous throws in previous games when deflections fell harmlessly away, but this time, his luck ran out.

The bigger concern was that Brian Schottenheimer and the offense didn’t have an effective counterpunch. CeeDee Lamb was completely neutralized. Tyler Smith returned but could not spark the running game, and even the later success involving George Pickens and Ryan Flournoy didn’t come easily, as both of them had to make incredible catches in traffic. Sadly, this team cannot survive if they experience any type of lingering offensive drought.

That is because of the real problem with this football team. The major problem. The Cowboys’ defense. There is no nice way to articulate it. This unit is outright terrible right now.

The tackling has become sloppy and the coverage breakdowns have become straight-up embarrassing. Even when this team is hustling around looking as if they’re going to make a huge play, their grabby hands will come up empty and shifts into a big play for the opposing offense. And this is happening all the time.

It’s hard to explain why this is happening. It’s about as puzzling as why DaRon Bland can’t stay upright and is always tripping over the ground, allowing a receiver to graze in wide-open spaces. And that is what the secondary does. Receivers are left unattended, assignments are missed, and communication disappears at the worst possible time.

The most aggravating part is that they are showing no sign of improving. After the big play to Zay Flowers late in the game against the Baltimore Ravens that only took six seconds and cost them the game, you would expect such a thing to sting to the point where they would be like, never again! Instead, two games later, the Cowboys’ defense surrendered a completely inexcusable 3rd-and-21 conversion when they ever-so-desperately needed a stop.

And Tampa made it look easy. That makes it even more annoying. Opponents arrive with a plan, and the Cowboys spend the afternoon reacting to it. That seems like a pretty good indicator that a team is being outcoached.

We know things are bad, but where do the Cowboys go from here? That is difficult to answer because the offense still has enough talent to make noise. Prescott, Lamb, Pickens, a capable offensive line, and a functional rushing attack should form one of the league’s better groups. And they are on most days.

Expecting the offense to produce at a high level isn’t unreasonable. It is the minimum requirement if the Cowboys want to remain relevant. The problem is that there is almost no margin for error because of what is happening on the other side of the ball.

Dallas cannot casually take a few possessions off while the offense searches for answers, because the defense is not equipped to keep the game within reach. Every possession carries extra weight, and every stalled drive feels like the beginning of the end.

The defense must find a way to be better. Asking for a takeaway almost seems absurd. A takeaway? How about they just get a stop? Make tackles. Stay disciplined. Communicate assignments. Get the correct calls in. Get off the field on third down. If they could somehow just do some of the basic things, it would feel transformational.

The schedule will not wait, either. Tougher opponents and better quarterbacks are coming, and even modest progress may not be enough by then.

There are reasons for some hope. Joey Porter Jr. should help. Quinnen Williams is still a great player. And rookie defenders such as Caleb Downs, Jaishawn Barham, and Malachi Lawrence offer potential. The supply cabinet is not empty. They have some tools.

That’s what makes the current performance hard to excuse. Christian Parker and his staff must turn this talent into a defense that understands its responsibilities and executes them. The question is whether meaningful change can happen quickly enough. A late-season rise to mediocrity seems like the ceiling for this group, but it will likely be too little, too late.

And while Parker’s failures have been on full display, Schottenheimer’s leadership deserves scrutiny as well. We’re not talking about the trivial stuff. No one should be overly bothered by the failed two-point attempt or trotting Brandon Aubrey out there for a long field goal only for it to get blocked. Criticize the execution, not the decision.

The real concern with Schottenheimer is that he appears to believe this team is better than it has shown. His calm demeanor can keep him composed in a difficult post-game interview, but it also screams complacency when the same problems continue to happen.

That was one of the most frustrating traits of the Mike McCarthy era. The belief that Dallas was basically fine and only needed minor adjustments. It was often good enough to win regular-season games, but never good enough to accomplish anything significant.

Schottenheimer preaches accountability, yet the Cowboys keep repeating unaccountable football. At some point, there needs to be a sense of urgency. Nobody is asking him to throw furniture, but a little visible frustration would at least suggest the alarm is sounding inside the facility. Right now, the Cowboys look too comfortable with problems that should make everyone uncomfortable. And that’s not a good sign.

That leaves the Cowboys in an awkward place. It is hard to imagine this team making serious noise this season, but there should be urgency in identifying how they can improve and who the people are that are going to help them achieve that noise one day. Which young players can become dependable contributors? Who needs to be replaced? The Cowboys brought in plenty of new faces, and the remaining schedule should provide a clear evaluation period.

The positive is that there is enough talent to build around, but they are pressed for time. The Dak Prescott window is entering its final stages, so patience is not a luxury the organization can afford. The Cowboys have also borrowed more from future cap resources than they typically do. Fans want the front office to go all out. Well, they got it, but aggressive moves carry consequences when the wins do not follow.

That makes this season particularly disappointing. The division remains up for grabs, and nobody has taken firm control of the NFC, yet the Cowboys cannot take advantage. The road only gets tougher from here. For fans, all we can do is search for progress, guard our optimism, and prepare for more turbulent waters.

entry.content:
Things got a little better on Sunday morning for the Cowboys as the Eagles fell to the Jaguars thanks to late-game heroics from Jacksonville. Then, the Giants and Commanders game ended in a tie due to poor clock management from Washington. While a Commanders win would be preferable, it was a good Sunday for the Cowboys, all things considered.

To win the division, though, Dallas will have to start stringing together back-to-back wins. Back-to-back wins have been rare in the Schottenheimer era. All in all, we can enjoy a Sunday without the disappointment of Cowboys football.

Updated NFC East Standings: Wild NFL Sunday Benefits Cowboys After Week 5- Randy Gurzi, Sports Illustrated

Although Thursday night was an upsetting game for Cowboys fans, there is a silver lining after Sunday’s action. The rest of the NFC East is doing the Cowboys favors by giving them an opportunity to climb back into the division.

2. Philadelphia Eagles (2-3)

Right now, the Philadelphia Eagles have the tiebreaker over the Cowboys because they are 1-0 in the NFC East, compared to 1-1 for Dallas. They should be 3-2, however, after taking a lead against the Jacksonville Jaguars with eight seconds to play.

NFC East Is For Losers: Cowboys Joined By Incompetence Across Division – Adam Schultz, Yahoo Sports

The division is still wide open thanks to help from other teams. However, to take advantage of the lack of success from other teams, they will need to string together wins. A task they have only done once in the Schottenheimer era.

Add it up, and incredibly, all four NFC East teams played this weekend … and they combined for zero wins!

The division remains there for the taking, but …

Why can’t the Cowboys win back-to-back games? That is one question we are all asking in the aftermath of the 24-16 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday night.

Cowboys’ possession battle woes, ruinous defensive penalties among maddening Week 5 stats- Todd Brock, Cowboys Wire

It has been well documented that the Cowboys are the only team without a defensive interception this season. And in the moment they could have changed that and flipped the outcome of the Thursday Night Football game, they failed.

0: Interceptions by defense… on the year

DaRon Bland’s blatant drop in the fourth quarter likely would have given the Cowboys a go-ahead touchdown with under four minutes to play and might have sealed a Week 5 win, but it also would have snapped a rather ugly streak of futility.

5 Coaches Who Could Take the Cowboys to the Next Level- Cody Warren, Inside The Star

During a long week, it may be a good time to think about what if. Granted, Schottenheimer absolutely has time to turn the ship around, but if it doesn’t happen Jerry and the organization needs to think about what’s next.

1. Kirby Smart Has Earned the Top Spot

Smart’s two National Championships at the University of Georgia put him first on my list, but what happened between those two titles is interesting.

Georgia lost eight defenders to the 2022 NFL Draft, including five first round picks. The next team won another championship while allowing 16.0 points per game.

Christian Parker turning Matt Eberflus into a sympathetic figure is rock bottom- Jerry Trotta, The Landry Hat

No fan expected the Cowboys to go from worst to first defensively simply by hiring Christian Parker and getting an exciting new rookie safety. However, possibly regressing after a horrific 2025 defensive campaign seemed equally unlikely.

Former Cowboys wide receiver Jesse Holley echoed a similar sentiment, tweeting that “Parker is actually doing much less with much more, making his job performance worse than Matt Eberflus.”

Being a prisoner of the moment is natural after an embarrassing primetime loss. This isn’t that. There’s real credence to the idea that Parker has been worse than Eberflus.
